newsitem.title: USA: Not time yet for public debate on Fed goals - Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Not time yet for public debate on Fed goals - Jordan.

text.p: A Federal Reserve policymaker said on Sunday that it was premature to have a public debate on changing the Fed's monetary policy objectives even though such a move would enhance its credibility.
"We're not yet ready to have that debate in public," Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan told a meeting here of the Association of Private Enterprise Education.
In remarks to the meeting and later to reporters, Jordan said that the central bank has restored much of its lost credibility and has committed itself to the achievement of a stable currency.
But the Fed policymaker argued that more was needed.

"We continue to call for a change in the environment in which monetary policy is conducted," he said. "We believe that specific and verifiable objectives must be imposed on the monetary authority (by) ... the state."
However, he said that there is no consensus yet within the economics profession on what such objectives should be.

"The dialogue of defining the objectives of a monetary authority has not progressed sufficiently within the economics profession to allow a fruitful public debate about codifying that objective," Jordan said.

Under current law, the Fed is required to seek balanced economic growth with maximum employment and stable prices. It is also required to set out targets for the growth of the money supply to help achieve that.

Some Republican lawmakers, including Sen. Connie Mack of Florida, want to change the Humphrey-Hawkins Act to establish price stability as the Fed's sole goal and set out verifiable targets for achieving that.

But the Fed itself seems divided on whether such a change would be beneficial. Vice Chair Alice Rivlin just last week reiterated her support for the Humphrey-Hawkins Act and said that reduction of inflation should not be the Fed's only goal.

For his part, Jordan said that he was not commenting directly on Humphrey-Hawkins or any other statute governing Fed policy. But he acknowledged that the time for monetary targetting as a political discipline on the Fed had passed.

He also argued that the Fed should not return to what he called the failed policies of the past when it tried to influence real economic activity. "The failed attempts at influencing real economic activity during the late 1960's and in the 1970's are a clear warning," he said. "It is a policy that we must not repeat."
